subject: java
summary: Explains how inheritance, interfaces, and polymorphism are used in real-world Java code, including method dispatch tracing and design trade-offs between abstract classes and interfaces.
key_points: Method calls on overridden methods resolve to the runtime instance type, not the declared variable type.
Interfaces define capability contracts without implementation; abstract classes share common logic with subclasses.
Polymorphism allows uniform handling of different implementations through a shared type.
misconceptions: The declared variable type determines which overridden method runs at runtime.
Abstract classes and interfaces are interchangeable with no practical difference.
Omitting @Override has no consequences when overriding a parent method.
check_questions: What is the difference between extends and implements in Java?
When should you choose an interface over an abstract class?
If a variable is declared as a parent type but holds a subclass instance, which class's method executes?

fact_candidates: Java does not support multiple class inheritance but allows multiple interface implementation.
@Override annotation triggers a compile-time check for correct method signature.
practical_judgment_candidates: Choosing between interface and abstract class for a notification system design.
Deciding when to use super() in an overridden method.
error_interpretation_candidates: A method override silently becomes a new method due to a parameter type mismatch.
NullPointerException caused by uninitialized inherited field.
scenario_candidates: Tracing which send() implementation executes in a polymorphic list iteration.
Reading a DI-based service class to identify its concrete dependency.
common_wrong_answer_patterns: Confusing compile-time type with runtime type for method dispatch.
Believing a subclass-specific method can be called through a parent-type variable without casting.
